title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
formal: For each integer \(k\ge 1\), determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points and every initial placement \(C_{0}\), there are a deterministic online rule A and a finite \(\beta \ge 0\) such that \(\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma ;C_{0})\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma ;C_{0})+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)}. Use the serving model below.
definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request \(r_{t}\) must be served before \(r_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server is already at \(r_{t}\), no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to \(r_{t}\), paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from \(C_{0}\) with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive \(\beta\) must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied. The ratio r depends only on k. The rule and additive constant may depend on the entire metric, \(k, C_{0}\) and r, but not on future requests or sequence length. The classical universal finite upper bounds make the infimum finite. It need not be achieved by one rule at its endpoint.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all integers \(k\ge 1\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

progress.text: Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator formulate the server framework, give the deterministic lower bound k, and resolve the two-server case on general metrics.
Chrobak and Larmore attain deterministic competitive ratio k on tree metrics.
Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove the general \((2k- 1)\) guarantee for the work-function algorithm; STOC 1994 is followed by the JACM 1995 paper.
Huang and Zhang settle work-function 3-competitiveness on circles. The May 2022 preprint appears in TCS on 12 December 2024.
Bubeck, Coester and Rabani publish the \(\Omega (\log ^{2}k)\) randomized lower bound, disproving the randomized \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture without refuting deterministic k-competitiveness.
Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé release a potential-discovery benchmark. The four-server circle experiments and finite inequality checks do not resolve the conjecture.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary source retains the deterministic conjecture and the general \((2k- 1)\) upper bound. The 2023 randomized disproof concerns \(O(\log  k)\), not the deterministic factor k. This card fixes all finite request sequences, identical initial placements, exactly k servers and an additive constant independent of requests; it asks for any deterministic online rule, not specifically WFA. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the function giving the best deterministic competitive ratio as the number of servers varies. The k-server conjecture predicts \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) together with a strategy attaining that ratio; the infimum formulation by itself does not demand endpoint attainment.

The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is \((2k- 1)\)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. That stronger statement would identify \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) using the known lower bound, while the quantitative target also permits other values. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega (\log ^{2}k)\). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and \(\log ^{2}k\) is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the \((2k- 1)\) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is the cost or competitive ratio of serving requests without knowledge of the future.

sentences: In k-server, requests arrive at points of a metric space and a server must move to each requested point.
The target is the infimum universal deterministic competitive ratio as a function of k.
The ratio is uniform over metric spaces, while the rule and fixed additive cost may depend on the metric and initial placement.
The classical k-server conjecture proposes the value k and attainment of that guarantee.
The Lean benchmark accepts a function within absolute error 0.01 for every positive integer k.
